design: P2.1 deliberate real-OOM demonstrations. NOT part of the replicated 10-rep dataset (results/real/*__cgroup.json); one-off runs specifically to obtain at least one real, measured time_to_oom_s, since it is null in every row of both the Windows/psutil and the replicated Linux/cgroup datasets. All rows is_synthetic:false.

v1_oversized_body.note: Python HTTP server (py_http_server.py) did NOT die under memory pressure across 3 attempts at increasing severity (10MB/8x@280m cap, 100MB/8x@250m, 300MB/16x@200m) -- peak_rss plateaued exactly at the container memory.max in every attempt, process survived, no kernel OOM-kill. Reported honestly as a real, non-null finding: this server's allocation pattern (Python bytes objects backed by malloc()) lets the OS return ENOMEM, which Python's stack turns into a catchable condition rather than an unresolvable page fault, so cgroup memory pressure here manifests as throttling/degradation, not a kill.

v3_unbounded_stdio.note: Node/TypeScript stdio server (ts_stdio_server.mjs) WAS reliably killed by the kernel's cgroup-v2 OOM killer: 3/3 runs at 500MB unbounded-line payload against a 150MB memory.max cap ended in SIGKILL (exit code -9) within ~0.07-0.13s of the attack starting. V8's heap growth touches newly-committed pages for the first time as the incoming stream is concatenated; a first-touch page fault cannot be answered with an error code the way a Python malloc() call can, so when the kernel can't reclaim enough to satisfy it, it must kill a process in the cgroup -- and it kills the memory-hogging Node server, not the (separate, tiny) Python driver process, so the measurement survives to record it.
